CausalChain: Chronic liver injury/dysfunction -> Altered albumin and bilirubin levels (high bilirubin, low albumin) -> Disruption of bile acid metabolism -> Gut microbiota dysbiosis -> Increased translocation of microbial products and inflammatory mediators -> Chronic hepatic inflammation -> Upregulation of immune checkpoint expression (e.g., PD-L1) -> Enhanced tumor immune evasion and progression -> Altered response to immunotherapy
Hypothesis: In HCC, abnormal ALBI grade is not merely a prognostic surrogate for liver reserve but also actively contributes to tumor progression and immune evasion by modulating bile acid–driven gut microbiome alterations and hepatic immune checkpoint pathways, thereby affecting the efficacy of immunotherapeutic interventions.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is strongly influenced by underlying liver dysfunction, traditionally assessed by composite scores such as ALBI. While ALBI grade is widely recognized as a robust prognostic indicator, emerging evidence suggests that its constituent parameters—albumin and bilirubin—may have direct biological roles beyond liver reserve assessment. We propose a novel hypothesis in which alterations in albumin and bilirubin levels, as captured by the ALBI grade, modulate bile acid homeostasis, thereby affecting gut microbiota composition and promoting a pro‐inflammatory environment in the liver. This cascade may further influence the hepatic immune microenvironment, including the expression of immune checkpoint molecules such as PD‐L1, and ultimately impact HCC progression and responsiveness to immunotherapy. This hypothesis encourages investigations into the gut–liver axis as a mechanistic link between liver function biomarkers and tumor immunobiology.
